chosen.title: Thinking in a Dish: How Lab-Grown Neurons Became the World's First Living Computers
chosen.rationale: Wetware computing hit real commercialization in 2026 — Cortical Labs' CL1 (the first commercial biological computer) and FinalSpark's cloud of 16 human brain organoids are now rentable, running ~1,000,000x more efficiently than silicon neurons. It's exactly Kenji's cybernetics/bioengineering beat: a vivid, mechanism-rich frontier with a built-in honest reckoning (consciousness ethics), and it's distinct from the covered BCI piece — this is growing neurons to compute, not wiring a human brain to a machine.

rejected_candidates.title: Teaching the Star to Behave: How AI Learned to Tame Fusion Plasma
rejected_candidates.rationale: 2026 is the year AI moved from the fusion lab bench toward the reactor — deep reinforcement learning (DeepMind/EPFL on TCV, the DIII-D tearing-instability controller) now steers plasma with millisecond magnetic tweaks, and the DOE's Genesis Mission is building AI-ready datasets to push toward commercial net gain. Perfect Kenji clean-energy + AI story: contagious wonder about controlling a miniature sun, grounded by an honest 'net-gain isn't confirmed yet' reckoning, and untouched by any covered energy piece (which cover carbon and microbial batteries, not fusion).

rejected_candidates.title: The Shapes No Human Would Draw: How Generative AI Is Redesigning What Machines Can Print
rejected_candidates.rationale: Additive manufacturing crossed a threshold in 2026: generative-design algorithms now output load-bearing geometries no engineer would sketch, CNNs catch defects at 99%+ in real time, and green-laser systems finally print copper/gold — Boeing, GE Aviation and BMW report 50–90% cost and weight savings. This lands squarely on Kenji's 3D-printing / advanced-manufacturing / maker-culture beat and speaks directly to the 'I could build this' audience, with no overlap on the covered autonomous-materials-lab piece.
